subject: Architecture
title: International Style: Glass Boxes Take Over
description: A quick win: understand International Style: Glass Boxes Take Over.

hook.text: After World War II, cities around the world filled with identical glass-and-steel boxes.

buildup.text: Mies van der Rohe's motto 'less is more' became the rule: no ornament, no curves, no decoration.

discovery.text: The Seagram Building in New York set the template: a bronze-tinted glass tower on a raised plaza.

twist.text: Every city copied the look. Critics said you could be in Tokyo, Lagos, or São Paulo and see the same skyline.

climax.text: The style was democratic in theory — but created some of the most soulless corporate towers ever built.

punchline.text: Less is more — until every city looks the same.

quiz.question: Who coined the phrase 'less is more' in architecture?

details.summary: The International Style standardized modern architecture into glass, steel, and concrete boxes with flat roofs, open floor plans, and zero ornament. Dominant from the 1930s through the 1970s, it gave cities worldwide a uniform look — clean and rational to admirers, cold and monotonous to critics.
details.whyItMatters: The International Style reshaped every major city skyline. Its universal approach made architecture efficient and democratic but also sparked the backlash that produced postmodernism and the diversity debate still active today.
takeaways: Glass, steel, and concrete boxes defined the International Style
It dominated global architecture from the 1930s to 1970s
Critics called it cold and monotonous; admirers praised its clarity

faq.question: Who coined the term International Style?
faq.answer: Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson named it in their 1932 exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. They identified three principles: volume rather than mass, regularity rather than symmetry, and the rejection of applied decoration.

faq.question: Why do so many office buildings look the same?
faq.answer: The International Style made glass curtain walls cheap and efficient, and developers adopted them worldwide. Mies van der Rohe's Seagram Building became the template — a rectangular glass-and-steel tower that could be replicated in any city regardless of climate or culture.
